text: Taking Linear Algebra this semester felt like dragging myself back to rusty ground in the middle of a sprinting term, and I’m glad Dr. Chen kept the big ideas clear even as I chased late-night notes. The explanations are strong conceptually, but the examples barely scratch the surface and I kept tripping over the platform quirks that make submitting things feel fiddly and stressful, which felt unnecessary given the workload. The grading rubric still feels vague to me, like I’m guessing whether a solution needs a matrix factorization step or a quick eigenvalue justification, and that didn’t help when I was racing against deadlines. I did skim the forums and office hours, found a small pointer there about how to phrase certain proofs, and that helped just enough to keep my sanity around a tricky late-week quiz. Overall, I can’t fully recommend it, but there was value in rebooting some rusty skills for my specialization.

I took Cyber Security Basics mid‑semester when I really needed this for the specialization, and the lectures—recorded—are useful but a bit dry, especially during a heavy week. The LMS and submission flow are smooth, which helps when the pace is already chaotic, but I remember one early confusion about the threat model that made me doubt I was in the right class for a while. Peer discussions tend to be more helpful than the official materials, and I often found myself relying on a quick back-and-forth in the forums, even if some responses felt dismissive. Overall, it’s okay for keeping up with the core content, and by now I’m juggling practice questions and a couple of project ideas instead of just lecture notes.

Operating Systems with Dr. Park felt like a mostly solo slog for me, since collaboration was minimal and the workload piled up, even though TAs were responsive and practical when I asked. The lectures never quite matched the assessment mix, and policies were fine but communications were sloppy, which added to the friction. I’d only recommend it if you’re comfortable with proofs and ready to push through the tougher weeks, especially around the exams. One memorable week was the big midterm, which felt oddly detached from the weekly forums.

Calculus II came on the calendar in my first semester here, and I stuck with it mainly because it fit my schedule more than because I was wildly excited about sequences and series. The lecturer has a knack for the big ideas; when we talked about convergence, the explanations clicked in a conceptual way even if the meat of the examples felt thin at times. I did have enough time to work through problems, but my motivation wavered inconsistently, so I often came away with more questions than solutions. The tool setup for the coursework was frustrating—getting the online grader and the submission portal to talk to each other felt like a minor hostage situation, which sapped energy before I even started. On the bright side, the TAs were responsive and pragmatic, usually pointing me to a workable path in office hours, which I did visit once after a noisy week at work. There were only a few assessments, yet each one felt like it mattered a lot; a single tricky midterm problem or a stubborn integration trick could tilt my grade more than I expected. Overall, I’m glad I pushed through the pacing, and I’ll remember the one office-hours chat where we mapped out a plan for the hardest chapter, even if the course left me with mixed feelings and some unfinished math in mind.

I came into Operating Systems expecting a challenging, rigorous elective, and I’ll admit I left with mixed feelings and a lot of questions. The first few weeks, I remember an early confusion about process scheduling that already framed how I viewed the rest of the term, and that lagged into every assignment. Prof. Rios explains concepts well at a high level, but the concrete examples were thin, and with my full-time job I always felt I needed more practice problems than the lectures offered. Quick feedback helped a bit, and I did manage to adjust after the weekly checkpoints, but the overall assessment mix didn’t sit right with me—there was a lot of theory and not enough hands-on problems that map to what we actually build. I think the course assumes more prior knowledge than advertised, which strained my time budgets, especially on the big project where I wish details about the grader’s expectations had been clearer. I remember a small incident during a debugging session in office hours that made me doubt whether I could keep up, and that doubt stuck around. Overall, I’d say it’s a tough ride with some useful ideas, but I’m still unsure if I’d take it again.

The Operating Systems course was a required slog that I somehow kept up with, mostly because I had to for the degree and because the lectures happened in short evening sessions that fit my schedule. I remember that first week I froze on a simple concept in process scheduling and it just stuck with me, shaping how I thought about the rest of the term even when the rest of the material felt like a blur. The peer discussion helped more than the official readings ever did, especially when the online forums were a bit dismissive about questions that seemed obvious to me. There weren’t many graded items, but each one felt heavy—a couple of short quizzes and a final project that loomed, so I ended up overpreparing in a way that didn’t feel efficient. The platform had quirks that added unnecessary stress, like quirks in assignment submission and a few flaky auto-grades, which didn’t help when I was juggling a tight evening study window. I liked the instructor, viewed as fair, but I disliked the grading approach enough that it colored the whole term for me, and I’m still not sure I’m fully aligned with how the marks were awarded.

tbh i took this intro ML class while working a full-time job and juggling maybe an hour or two most weeks, and i barely scraped by. grading felt fairly transparent when it finally landed, but the feedback arrived so late i could barely use it to improve before the next deadline, which left me feeling stuck half the term. the course itself felt uneven week to week, like some weeks we’d dive into a neat intuition and other weeks we’d get tangled in a slide pile with sparse explanations, which didn’t help my limited study time. i appreciated that the material actually filled some gaps in prerequisites better than i expected, and i think prof. alvarez did a solid job mapping basics to the kind of projects you’ll see in practice, but i still ended up needing to lean on office hours more than i’d hoped; i remember one hour where we worked through a failing model in a notebook and it finally clicked, which kept me going. the deadline pattern and the one project felt a bit brittle, but i’d still recommend the course to someone who can prep a bit ahead and use those quiet pockets of feedback.

Last semester felt like I kept chasing a clock I couldn’t see, and the main glare was Dr. Chen’s lecture pace in Linear Algebra. The feedback arrived fast, but the explanations behind it were thin, so I never quite felt like I understood whether I was off or right, just that I was missing something. The course is an advanced elective, and with only a handful of assessments, each one carried serious weight, which made every mistake sting more than it should have in a math class. I compared it a lot to the prerequisite that felt almost easy in hindsight, and I kept thinking, if that intro stuff clicked so easily, why did the jump to this material feel like navigating with dim headlights? Peer discussions helped more than the official slides or the problem sets, which is odd to admit, but true—group chats often solved the trickier parts long after the lecture. Email support was slow during deadlines, which left me scrambling when a deadline collided with a busy week. There was a small project toward the end that I actually found useful, but overall I’m not sure the grade—C, and I’m still unsure if that reflects my understanding. It’s not a clean yes or no to recommending it.

I’m juggling Data Structures as a required course for my track, and with a full-time job in software support, I had to fit study around short evening sessions. The first few weeks were okay—Dr. Chen starts accessible enough, but the workload ramps up fast, and the weekly problem sets feel engineered to test you under time pressure more than to teach the core ideas. The report-heavy assessments are what eat my evenings: recurring big write-ups and a midterm project that drags on due to data structure tracing and edge-case tests. TAs are responsive and practical, which helps when I’m stuck after hours, and I did appreciate the quick feedback on my submission scores, even if the explanations were thin. I remember a concrete moment in office hours when a TA walked me through debugging why a linked list reversal caused a null-pointer in a corner case, which was a small relief after a long day. A lot of it comes down to fit—it starts manageable and then the pace and the grading quirks become the real challenge, but I’d still recommend it to others who can carve out focused evening blocks.

Took Database Systems in my first semester and I learned a lot, but I still think the course dragged me down a bit because the difficulty was higher than I expected and I often felt kind of stretched by the crunch mid‑semester. The lectures with Prof. Haddad were clear enough on the concepts, and the LMS submission flow was smooth, which helped when deadlines piled up, but the prerequisites felt a bit off for me—some basics didn’t click and I felt I wasn’t fully aligned with what was assumed. The report-heavy workload took ages, and even though the feedback came fast, the explanations behind the scores were pretty thin, so I wasn’t sure how much I actually understood my mistakes. I had enough time overall, but my motivation was inconsistent, and that made the whole thing feel like a slog rather than a coherent learning arc. There were a few moments where I felt I learned a lot, then the next assignment would overwhelm me with interpretation-heavy instructions that left too much room for guesswork. I’m not sure I’d call it a solid match for me, and I’m uncertain whether I’d recommend it to someone else. The mix of frustration and insight sticks with me, especially that rough mid‑semester crunch.

I kept up with nearly every lecture, but the grading felt opaque and tighter than expected for a solid B given the effort with a full-time job. The official materials didn’t help much; I relied on forum threads and chatting with the TA during office hours more than the slides. The few assessments mattered a lot, and the tooling setup was frustrating, especially when syncing notebooks and datasets before a deadline week. The instructor was engaging, but the grading vibe didn’t match the lively class discussions.

Cyber Security Basics felt like a mixed ride: I learned a ton, but the experience dragged in some stubborn ways. Prof. Alvarez is clearly solid, but the vibe is more neutral than inspiring, and the lectures don’t always land as clearly as I hoped given my strong coding background and comparatively weaker theory. The course leaned heavy on assignments with frequent deadlines, which suiting my schedule but made the weeks feel like a sprint, especially when the official feedback was detailed yet slow to arrive. I mostly relied on recordings and notes, and the tool setup ate more time than I’d like, so I’d crawl through a lot of setup stuff before even starting the core tasks. A standout help moment was office hours; the TA and Prof. Alvarez sometimes rescued the week when I got stuck on a cryptography-style problem or a tricky lab scenario, and those sessions felt practical. I compare it to the prerequisite that was easier, and I remember thinking this one demanded more theory than I expected, even as I still managed to push through with my coding instincts. Overall, I learned a lot, but I can’t shake the sense that the experience itself was a bit grueling and imperfect.

I took Data Structures last summer while juggling a full-time job, and I’ll admit the pace felt brutal for someone with a solid coding background but weak theory—the lectures came across as dry, even with the recordings available, and I found myself skimming through to catch the practical bits. The big turning point came late in the term when we finally shipped a group project that required actually reasoning about memory layouts under load; that moment clicked because the team dynamics started to matter more than the individual lectures, and we started interrupting our own blind spots to cover for each other. Setup for the tooling was a constant bottleneck—the IDE extensions and build scripts ate more time than the learning payoff, and I’m still not sure if that was the course design or my own mismatch with the workflow. Prerequisites felt heavier than advertised, like I needed a deeper theoretical grounding to really follow the proofs they skimmed in class, which made the compressed summer term feel even harsher. Group work helped when the team functioned, but when someone spiraled into last-minute patches, it dragged us all down, so the value was unevenly distributed. Overall, a solid B matched the effort, with enough rough edges to stick in memory for a while.

Midway through the heavy semester, I’m finding Data Structures with Dr. Park is more relevant in theory than in practice for real work, especially since this is supposed to be an introductory service course. The quick feedback helps me adjust, but the grading rubric still feels vague, which leaves a lot of room for interpretation on what exactly counts as a good submission. I came in hoping it’d be a toolkit for industry, and while the office hours rescue the course when I’m stuck, it’s clear the class flows best if you’re in a study group and share notes. A project and a couple of deadline quirks stick with me more than the lectures themselves, and I’m left mentally exhausted despite the appears-fair assessment. Overall, it’s usable but not as cleanly aligned with what I expected.

The software stack starts rough and looks like a slog, but you loosen up after a couple of weeks; still, you need adjacent material already clear in your head to feel comfortable. The vibe is more student-to-student help than staff guidance, and I learned a lot in practice, but I still wouldn’t recommend it—there’s value, just not the calm, reliable track you’d want in a mid-program core.

Calculus II with Prof. Alvarez felt like a mixed back-and-forth: I kept telling myself it was the prerequisites that were the problem, not the class, but I still fell behind and then tried to sprint to catch up right before the deadlines. The materials were solid—clear notes, decent problem sets, and a couple of useful lecture recordings that saved my sanity when I was juggling other courses—but the assessment design wore me down: a lot of report-heavy, time-consuming tasks that felt like grading by word count rather than clarity of understanding, which left me wondering if my grasp of the concepts was fair to gauge or if I was just grinding through the paperwork. Pacing was neutral in practice; some weeks dragged, other weeks I was scrambling to hit a moving target, and I compared it unfavorably to the easier prerequisite that felt more forgiving. I mostly worked solo, with little peer dependency, which made the collaboration structure feel oddly isolating even though the topics clicked in class. Attendance patterns weren’t pretty for a while, but I did manage to catch up around deadlines, and honestly I’m unsure whether the C reflected my actual understanding or just the grading tilt for the big reports.

This OS course through Dr. Singh felt like a rough start to the semester: I’m comfortable with proofs, but the systems stuff and tooling setup dragged on longer than it should have, and the setup friction gnawed at motivation more than once. The materials were fine in a neutral way, not flashy, but the prerequisites felt a bit optimistic for someone approaching it from a pure math/logic angle. Feedback came in fits and starts, and by the time I actually got notes on the last project I was already worried about the next deadline. I found the course works better if you team up with a study group, the shared problem-solving helps when the pacing isn’t smooth, and there was one late-semester turning point that finally clicked for me, even as I still felt exhausted by the end.

I’m here because I needed this for a specialization, but the assignment-heavy pace and delayed feedback left me stuck; still, I learned enough to see why the prerequisite felt easier in retrospect. The group chats helped more than the staff did, and the actual grading comments were detailed, just later than I needed.

I took Database Systems hoping it’d feel practical for industry work, but I left with mixed feelings and a rough mid-semester crunch that threw off my momentum. Dr. Chen is solid in lectures, yet the prerequisite feel like more than what was promised, and I found myself relying mostly on recordings and notes rather than live class energy. I’d only recommend taking it if you’re prepared to put in extra prep and tolerate a bit of sloppy communication on administrative bits, plus don’t expect a tidy payoff.

Dr. Chen’s Operating Systems course was okay to start, but I’m unsure whether the grade reflected my real understanding. The intro service-course vibe meant I could tell the material tried to fill gaps, and the prerequisites fit better than I expected, though I still felt shaky when we hit process scheduling concepts. The biggest hassle wasn’t the ideas themselves but the tooling and deadline rhythm: a lot of the deadlines slid into weeks with weird, inconsistent tool quirks that made the weekly deliverables feel like a moving target, and even when feedback scores came fast, the explanations were thin and left me guessing what to fix. Collaboration expectations were vague, which meant my partner and I wasted time trying to infer who was supposed to do what, and I ended up doing more solo work while juggling a full-time job. I managed time but motivation ebbed and flowed, so some weeks I pushed through on instinct rather than clear guidance. There was one project involving a small kernel module where a missing debug flag suddenly blew a milestone, and that stickiness stuck with me. Overall I’m not sure I’d recommend it as a clean pathway to solid OS intuition, but it’s not a total wash either.

Going into Cyber Security Basics last semester before graduation, I expected something that would bridge theory with real systems, but I mostly found it feel like a slog of proofs without the practical pull I needed. The quick feedback helped me adjust, and the LMS flow was smooth enough that I didn’t worry about submitting late or losing points, which was a relief. I’m comfortable with the proofs side, but on the systems stuff, the hands-on parts didn’t click the way I hoped, and the practical application felt more theoretical gymnastics than usable know-how in the real world. The course policies are fine, but communication was sloppy at times—like when a deadline shift didn’t get communicated clearly and I ended up scrambling to re-prioritize my week. Most work was solo, with little peer dependency, so I didn’t get that collaborative push I expected from electives, which left me tracing steps on my own. One moment sticks: an office-hours thread where I described a misconfiguration I’d been chasing for days and the TA pointed me to a config snippet that finally made sense, which was small but oddly satisfying in the middle of a tense term. Overall, it’s competent but not what I needed for concrete, deployable skills.
